source.title: Beyond Token-Level Guidance: Inference-Time Alignment of Specialized LLMs via Cross-Family Representation Steering
source.authors: Jin Gan; Xin Li; Jun Luo

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper uses representation-space safety steering as a tool for aligning specialized models, but it does not test the original difference-in-means refusal direction or the claim versions. Its safety results evaluate CREST, a different, conditional steering method.
record.gate_note: The paper cites the original study in related work, but reports no new test of its refusal direction. CREST derives query-specific directions using a safe-prompt prefix and a partial generation, maps them across models with Procrustes alignment, and steers selected layers for a limited number of tokens. Its reported safety outcomes are results of that deliberately applied method, not evidence that the original single direction mediates refusal. Table 1's EOS-suppression results concern token-level guidance, not the claimed refusal direction.
record.test_reason: CREST steers specialized models with query-specific safety directions from a separate guidance model, built from a safe prefix and a probe generation and mapped across models by Procrustes alignment. It does not extract, ablate or add the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction in the model under study. The safety numbers measure the performance of the authors' own deliberately applied method. Arditi et al. is cited only in related work.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also claim to identify 'complementary expertise orthogonality' as the root cause of token-level methods' failure, through end-of-sequence suppression. They report CREST's latency as 1.3× base-only.
record.recipe_differences: CREST uses Procrustes alignment to map guidance-model representations, a query-specific direction based on a safe-prompt prefix and the base model's probe generation, and conditional steering of selected layers for a limited intervention window. It does not use the original harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction, project that direction out at all layers and positions, or add it to induce refusal.
record.method_sensitivity: CREST results vary with guidance-model choice in the reported sensitivity table; the paper also reports CREST-specific sweeps over steering strength, probe length, steered layers, intervention length, and detection threshold.

fits_no_version.finding: Cross-family representation steering, with directions taken from a guidance model, modestly improves safety on code (0.18→0.14) and math (0.92→0.96) specialized models with negligible capability change. Medical stays at 0.99, and results vary by guidance model.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Safety directions from an aligned guidance model can be Procrustes-mapped into a specialized model of another family to restore some safety degraded by fine-tuning, without capability loss.

record.problems: The paper states that capability comparisons against token-level baselines are indirect because the methods use different generation backends. Safety scoring for math and medical relies on GPT-4o-mini, and the appendix reports sensitivity to answer extraction, especially for medical. No uncertainty estimates are stated for the reported benchmark results.
record.rows_left_out: CREST-specific parameter sweeps in Appendix A.3 (Tables 3–6 and 8) were not extracted because they tune CREST rather than test the claimed refusal direction. Table 1's token-level EOS-suppression and buried-answer results were also left out because they do not measure the claimed refusal direction or its predicted refusal behavior.

untested.parts: No ablation or addition of the difference-in-means refusal direction, and no measurement of refusal induced on harmless prompts.
No jailbreaks; the authors place adversarial robustness out of scope.
Harm judgment and refusal are not separated.
Cross-family transfer is of CREST's own per-query directions, not of the refusal direction.
Specialization fine-tuning degrades safety, but whether a removable refusal direction exists is not tested.
No reasoning-model analysis of the direction.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T4 / uses_without_test classification is right. No verdicts are given because no row bears on any version. The study argues that self-derived refusal directions may be unreliable after specialization fine-tuning, but it gives no test of this. The hyperparameter sweeps and the end-of-sequence tables were correctly left out.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate or add the harmful-minus-harmless difference-in-means refusal direction; does not test refusal on harmless requests or whether the claimed direction preserves general abilities.
No weight edit or abliteration is evaluated.
No jailbreak attack is tested as suppressing the claimed direction, and no training against its ablation is performed.
Does not compare a single direction with an affine, cone, or multi-direction account of refusal.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.

CREST transfers its own safety representations across model families, but does not test whether the claimed difference-in-means refusal direction transfers across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models.
Evaluates specialized models but does not test how or when refusal training determines whether the claimed removable direction exists.
Does not test the claimed direction in reasoning models.
